source: There, there. Have a seat.
What can I get you two ladies?
The largest flagons of wine you can manage, sir...
Call me Othello. Done, and done.
You have that look about you—women troubled by men. Which is a look I see every day in this bar.
It's her former lover. He's gone stark raving mad.
Did you see the way he was carrying on, Rosie? That strange, twitchy look in his eye?
He's certainly changed quickly.
Say, Rosie, you don't think he...
Absolutely. I was thinking exactly that.
But if that's true, then...
Oh, my goodness.
How dare he!
I cannot believe him.
Er. I've missed a crucial piece somewhere.
What are you talking about? Who is 'he'? What has 'he' done?
(And how do they know what in hell the other one's talking about...?)
W-well, you see, Guilda and this man... have a long history.
And it's not like him to act the way he did when we spoke to him.
He's hanging on to some secret. And we're not sure what it might be.
Or maybe we are, because that secret...
...Is that he's in love with someone else.
These things have a way of happening, my ladies.
Othello, what would you do if someone you loved found a new love of their own?
Me? Well, to be certain, I've never loved all that deeply.
I'd prefer to think I have a free and open nature. I think men honest who seem to be so.
Someone once told me I was easy to lead around, like a donkey...
So I suppose I'd try to support the new union as best I could. Seems only fair, doesn't it?
If you love that person, then you love the very act of them loving, because it brings them great happiness.
And if the target of their love isn't you... then you must relinquish your feelings for the sake of their happiness.
But... that's... so sensible and mature!
I'm far too petty to think like that, ordinarily.
(And according to Quince, so is Othello, in reality...)
You're a little wiser than you look, humble barkeep.
He's right, though. Hamlet owes me nothing.
Whatever's going on in his mind, he clearly has thought little of me lately.
Then you should think only of yourself, too.
Find someone new to love.
Oh, that's all right, Rosie. You know I only ever really have eyes for you, in the end.
And I for you, my little shadow.
Cheers. I'll drink to that.
To new love!
To forgetting old love!
And to friendship!
Old man, oughtn't you to be on duty?
Aye! I could ask you the same, hag.
This is why yer supper-stew always smells like 'alf a casket of wine, ain't it? Yer down here drinking!
Leave me to my vices. In my old age, they're the only friends I have.
Well, well! An' here I thought we were friends.
You? Bah. Never.
What are you doin' here anyhow?
Came to see m' gran'daughter. The babe's not a babe any longer. She's walkin' now.
You have children?
Thirteen of 'em!
You never spoke of them. How do you feed all of those mouths?
Well, now that they're grown, they feed themselves jes' fine. But yeh know, there were some rough years.
Before my sweet Isabella passed, she ran all thirteen of 'em like a military regiment.
She had t'older ones watch th'younger ones, an' all of them tilled the land an' ran the household.
She wos a lot like you, come t'think of it. A real bag o' nails.
Mind your tongue. There's still enough lady left in me to be offended.
How old is the youngest child now?
Fourteen. She's gone an' gotten married, too. Makin' her father proud.
That's Anna. My oldest, Alexander, 'e's got grey at 'is temples, just like me.
Alexander? As in...
Aye. King Alexander. Th'first man I ever served in Elsinore, an' the greatest.
My lady Gertrude seems to believe... he was rather a cruel man.
The greatest, and the cruelest. Where d'you think Hamlet an' Claudius got their mean streak?
Ah, Alexander beat 'em without a second thought if they weren't polished an' hardy at all times!
But yeh know, he applied that same work to all th'men who served 'im in the wars. Myself included.
It made us all th'better. We were made o' steel! We fought like hell! We sent our enemies packin' a dozen times.
An' his rewards were all the sweeter. Casks o' wine so fat and round, three men wiv hands joined couldn't surround 'em.
King Alexander sure knew how to discipline 'em like the best. I wos proud to name my son after 'im.
Such a pity and a shame to see his grandson behaving as he does. I wonder what King Alexander would say.
Well, yeh know. Even the best tree produces a weird-lookin' fruit now an' then.
A weird-looking fruit, indeed, that one.
What o' yourself? Where are yer children now?
My husband died not long after I discovered I was with child. He fell under a horse cart and was trampled.
But I swore to build a great family, to move forward even as I prayed for his immortal soul.
I bore my daughter. Marie.
She was a sickly little thing. Hardly the size of my hand when she was born. And she didn't cry.
I thought that made her a peaceful child. I remember marveling to the doctor--'isn't she a wonder, my quiet child?'
But it was bad, the silence. It meant her lungs were weak. She made a faint rattling sound when she breathed.
The night Marie was born, Her Majesty Gertrude was born as well. Little Gerta, they called her.
Gertrude was a healthy child, but her mother made no milk. So they brought her to me.
I fed her and Marie at the same time, looking down at both their faces as I held them close.
Gerta cooed and smiled, and her eyes were curious, even then.
But my daughter Marie—she looked at nothing. She refused my breast. She moved little.
I watched one babe wither away and the other flourish.
One morning, I reached for my daughter, and her tiny body was cold. I called a priest.
They took her from me and buried her.
And I continued to feed Gerta, little Gerta, who grew larger every day.
And now Gerta is grown and married, every bit the graceful woman I knew she would become.
Aw, hell, Irma. I had no clue.
Yeh know...
If it makes yeh feel any better, you can steal all o' my money th'next time we play cards.
Hmm. The despairing look on all of your fat, ruddy faces when I fleece you does bring me great comfort.
Well, now, let's not get ahead o' ourselves, yeh evil hag.
Better evil than a clod.
'Ey, I'm proud t'be a clod. Bein' smart never did anyone no good.
Look at us. Two drunken old fools trading insults. We both have better places to be.
Eh. I'd rather stay here an' drink with you. I'll let Bernardo lecture me later.
Then... cheers. To the old, forgotten ones.
My spring, my joy, my day, my beloved, my laughing rose...
My delight, my wine, my tavern, my lamp, my light, my candle...
And what have we here, Othello?
Ah, just a flight of fancy. The thing's out of tune.
Sounds tuned well enough to me.
And I do so love to be serenaded. Especially by the strong, silent type.
Me? Silent? You must be joking.
Hmm. Excellent point. Strong, then.
What would you like to hear?
Oh, there's a little old bit of something I heard in the barracks often...
The barracks? You, a soldier?
Ahh, believe it or not... once. Under King Hamlet in his infamous three-year chess match with Norway.
Three years is but a blink of an eye in a war, back where I come from.
When the countries are but a week's travel apart, a three-year conflict feels like eternity.
But I wasn't cut out for that life, I'm afraid. I much prefer reasonable discussion to endless posturing and saber-rattling.
And I much prefer to rattle a literal saber.
You have the look of an old soldier about you. In which war did you fight?
Which war? Why, the unending war the Turks wage upon all who do not bow to the Sultan.
I served at the Sultan's pleasure for over a decade and fought for his causes against foreigners. I beheaded thousands of men.
I find that strangely charming. And possibly seductive.
Hmph. Well, I'm certain there's many a man willing to... grab your head around here.
Toward the end of my decade, I was one of the Sultan's own viziers. I had gardens and treasures aplenty. This feels like a different world entirely.
You gave up all that to come to this rotten, pasty little country? Why on earth?
Because it was not truly mine. I was an Ottoman slave. Everything I did was in my master's name, even when I surpassed his rank with my own.
In fact, my master's name—'Halil'—was appended to my name quite literally. I longed to be my own man. So I fled.
I imagine you aren't welcome in Constantinople any longer.
I'm sure they would welcome me. Right into an execution chamber.
Heh. Well, with the way Denmark's trending, your fortunes may not be better here.
Aye. What a pity, that.
...At least we've still got music.
It is the only thing which transcends language or border.
Even dance may offend. But music is immortal.
I wish you excellent fortune in getting that lute to tune.
Thanks, friend. We'll see.
The time has come, my noble ladies. Hop to it.
T-t-this is exploitation!
Yes! This is humane!
You mean inhumane, Guilda.
That's what I said!
Need I remind you the sum of your debt to me?
Five years of losing every game you've played at my table. Plus interest.
I must be repaid, if I have to rip those fine dresses off you two and sell them!
We helped you find your ingredients earlier!
Feh! You think that is enough to make up your sum? Hardly!
It's true we've failed to pay Irma in the past...
But I must admit, I'd assumed she would have forgotten.
N-not to mention, I thought we'd have skipped town by now.
This was supposed to be a quick visit. Pay our respects and leave!
Enough! Now! Begin!
Ugh! Fine!
(You sing. I'll provide, er, emotional support.)
(Why am I always the singer?!)
D-deathless Aphrodite, throned in flowers...
Break my spirit, Lady, no longer!
Hear anew the voice! O hear and listen!
Come, as in that island dawn thou camest...
From thy father's golden house, hearing my pleading!
Uhm, how does the rest of it go?
You stood with a sudden brilliance, Goddess, before me...
You asked me what I suffered, who was my cause of anguish...
'Now she runs away, but she'll soon pursue you;'
